title: Hyperosmolar Therapy — HTS vs Mannitol
sources: Critical Vector — Hypertonic Saline vs Mannitol pocket reference (v1, verified vs Crit Care Med / Neurosurgery / Neurosurg Rev, July 2026)
Kamel H et al. Crit Care Med 2011 (equiosmolar RCT meta-analysis)
Gu J et al. Neurosurg Rev 2019 (12 RCTs, 438 pts)
Mangat HS et al. Neurosurgery 2020; pooled 18-trial synthesis 2020–2023 (1,828 pts)

changelog.change: Initial entry — converted from the CV HTS-vs-mannitol guide. Mechanism, the acute-window evidence nuance, dosing, safety hard-stops, and the volume-status-driven bedside decision.

summary: Both agents lower ICP by pulling free water across an intact blood-brain barrier. The clinically useful question is not which is better but which is safer for the patient's volume status, renal function, and sodium trajectory. Mannitol causes obligate diuresis (depletes volume); hypertonic saline expands volume.

body.text: This is specifically about the choice between the two agents. General ICP management (Monro-Kellie, herniation, Cushing's triad, CO2 reactivity) lives elsewhere. Most clinicians pick by habit rather than the patient's physiology — that's the gap this reference addresses.

rows: ~0.9 — some crosses an injured BBB over time, blunting the gradient
~1.0 — stays almost entirely intravascular even with BBB disruption; more durable gradient
Rheological — lowers blood viscosity, transiently improves CBF and O2 delivery; obligate diuresis
Volume expansion — raises intravascular volume and CPP, generally without diuretic loss
Depletes intravascular volume — a problem if already hypovolemic / hypotensive
Expands volume — an advantage in hypotension, a liability in volume overload (heart failure)

items: Gu 2019 (12 RCTs): HS and mannitol close on functional outcome (RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.89–1.54) and ICP reduction — no significant difference.

Mangat 2020: HS showed a superior combined ICP + CPP effect, with a significant CPP rise from baseline (63 → 76 mmHg at 120 min) not seen with mannitol — consistent with HS's volume-expansion mechanism.

Pooled 18-trial synthesis (1,828 pts): in the acute 30–60 min window HS showed a 62% reduction in treatment failure (OR 0.38, 95% CI 0.15–0.98), higher CPP, modestly lower ICP. By 90–120 min the effects attenuated and no consistent between-group difference remained (mortality, function, CPP, ICP).
Bottom line: HS's advantage is most consistent in the acute, early post-infusion window — not a durable sustained superiority. Whether HS confers a lasting outcome benefit is unresolved.

rows: 3%: 150–250 mL bolus or continuous infusion · 23.4%: 30 mL bolus (central line preferred)
3% peripheral generally acceptable; 23.4% preferably via CVC

body.text: The faster onset / shorter duration of HS maps onto the acute-vs-sustained evidence pattern — a faster agent showing its clearest advantage early, then converging with the slower, longer-acting agent at steady state.

rows: Hypotension and hypovolemia from obligate diuresis
Volume overload in underlying heart failure
AKI risk, especially with repeated dosing or in dehydrated / renal-compromised patients
Described, particularly with repeated dosing as the agent redistributes
Hypernatremia + volume overload if unmonitored; osmotic demyelination is a theoretical concern with rapid correction, though the acute-bolus context differs from chronic hyponatremia correction

body.text: Avoid mannitol in dehydrated, hypotensive, or renal-compromised patients — obligate diuresis compounds all three at once.
The bedside decision — which direction does this patient's volume status need to move?
